extracted.intended_audience: researchers and institutions who collaborate with Indigenous communities (and related policymakers/industry stakeholders)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for researchers, institutions and industry on ethical collaboration with Indigenous communities, including benefit-sharing, authorship credit, capacity building and negotiation of compensation for traditional knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensate Indigenous communities for their knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Indigenous communities must be compensated for their knowledge and treated as equals in research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rooibos agreement is presented as a landmark example: communities will receive 1.5% of the 'farm gate price'. The article frames compensation as a moral obligation, especially given histories of land loss and exploitation; it notes the agreement applies to an entire industry and took nine years to negotiate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be up front about research intentions
rubrics_metrics.description: The code urges scientists to be up front about their intentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: San communities’ code of ethics explicitly recommends clarity about researchers' aims at the outset to avoid misunderstandings, mistrust or exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow through on promises to share publication credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should follow through on promises to share publication credit with Indigenous contributors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ethics code calls for sharing credit; failing to do so is identified as a source of grievance. Sharing credit helps recognize intellectual contributions and supports equitable partnerships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build community capacity for Indigenous-led research
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, build community capacity for Indigenous groups to do their own studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ethics code recommends capacity‑building so communities can conduct research themselves, promoting long-term autonomy and sustained benefit rather than one‑off extraction of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat Indigenous people as equals and partners
rubrics_metrics.description: Indigenous people, especially those whose ancestors lost lives, land and livelihoods, should be treated fairly and as equals in research relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Working with communities as partners leads to more constructive relationships and mutual benefits; industry and researchers should adopt partnership models rather than hierarchical, extractive approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share benefits, not just access or data
rubrics_metrics.description: Research and commerce must share credit and the potential benefits with those who generated traditional knowledge, not only access to information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights that access to traditional knowledge alone, without benefit-sharing, is a core concern for communities. Benefit-sharing can include profit shares (as in rooibos), authorship, capacity, and other tangible returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid protracted intellectual-property contests; negotiate collaboratively
rubrics_metrics.description: Contesting the origins of traditional knowledge and intellectual-property claims can lead to prolonged stalemates and recriminations; more harmonious, collaborative negotiation is preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rooibos case took nine years partly because industry contested historical claims, commissioning its own study and prolonging dispute. Early, good‑faith negotiation and collaborative processes can prevent long delays and conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge evidentiary uncertainty but prioritize ethical remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when historical or scientific evidence about origins is open to interpretation, there remains a moral case to compensate long‑mistreated groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editorial notes that two reviews of the same literature can reach different conclusions; nonetheless, ethical considerations (redressing past exploitation) can and should guide responses despite evidentiary ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use policy and government mechanisms to broker fair agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments can and should play a role in brokering compensation agreements between industry and Indigenous communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the rooibos example, the government reviewed literature and advised the industry to pay the communities; policy intervention can facilitate equitable outcomes where voluntary arrangements stall.
